Play the game AI notes · July 2026

About the AIs

The world's oldest board game was solved last year. I only just found out.

I built AI opponents for the Royal Game of Ur in a burst of enthusiasm last summer — classical search first, then machine learning — and then let the project sleep. When I came back this month to freshen up the site, I learned the game had been solved the whole time. This is the story of three AIs, one overdue discovery, and what “solved” actually means.

Rob GilksJuly 20268 minute read

In the 1920s, Leonard Woolley's excavation of the Royal Cemetery of Ur — in what is now southern Iraq — turned up a handful of beautiful game boards: twenty squares of shell inlaid with lapis lazuli and red limestone, about 4,500 years old. We would have no idea how to play, except that Irving Finkel, a curator at the British Museum, deciphered a clay tablet written by a Babylonian scribe in 177 BCE — a rulebook, written down when the game was already older than chess is now. His reconstruction is the game people play today, which makes Ur arguably the oldest game on Earth we still know how to play properly.

You can play it right here, in your browser. Last summer, in a burst of enthusiasm, I built two computer opponents for it — one that searches, and one that imitates. Then the project slept for a year. This July I came back, intending only to refresh the site's look and feel, and instead ended up building a third opponent — one taught by perfection itself. The timeline explains why.

The game, in one minute

Ur is a racing game — backgammon's great-great-grandparent. Each player has seven pieces and wants to run them along a fixed track and bear them off the far end. Movement comes from four binary dice: tetrahedral dice with two of four corners marked, each one effectively a coin flip. A roll is 0 to 4, and the odds follow a coin-flip curve — you roll a 2 six times as often as a 0 or a 4.

The interesting part is the middle. Your track begins and ends on your own safe side of the board, but its central eight squares are shared with your opponent. Land on their piece there and it goes back to the start. Five squares carry a rosette: land on one and you roll again — and while you sit on it, you cannot be captured. Bearing off needs an exact roll.

That's the entire rule set, and it's enough to create genuine decisions: race or fight, spread out or stack up, grab the contested central rosette or slip past it. Luck arrives every single turn, but the choices compound. That mix — simple rules, dice, real strategy — is also what makes it a lovely test subject for game AI.

The first opponent: search

If you've read anything about chess engines, you know minimax: I pick my best move, assuming you'll pick your best reply, assuming I'll pick my best response to that, down to some depth — then I score the outcomes and choose accordingly. Dice break this. Between my move and your reply sits a roll that neither of us controls, so there is no single “your best reply” to plan against.

The fix is called expectiminimax, and it's the one idea I'd like you to take away for the price of this coffee break: wherever chance intervenes, insert a chance node whose value is the probability-weighted average of its children. My layers maximise, your layers minimise, and the dice layers simply take the expectation.

Classic, the first opponent, does exactly this — written in Rust, compiled to WebAssembly, searching three plies deep in your browser with alpha–beta pruning and a transposition table (a cache of positions it has already scored, because the same position recurs constantly). Three plies sounds shallow, but each one multiplies the tree by every legal move times five possible rolls, and the whole thing has to answer in about a millisecond on a phone.

When the search runs out of depth, it scores the position with a hand-designed evaluation function: eight weights covering advancement, captures, rosette control and so on. But how much is a capture worth, relative to a square of progress? Rather than guess, I let a genetic algorithm fight it out — fifty generations of fifty weight-sets, each judged over a hundred games, with a challenger replacing the champion only after winning more than 55% of a thousand-game final. My favourite detail of the whole project: evolution set the “safety” weight slightly negative. Given the choice, it would rather threaten than hide.

The second opponent: imitation

The second opponent has the fashionable shape: two small neural networks, in the arrangement AlphaGo made famous — a value network (“who's winning here?”) and a policy network (“which piece would you move?”). Mine are modest, about 164,000 parameters between them, and they weren't trained on human games or by reinforcement learning. They were trained to imitate Classic. I simulated six thousand games, labelled nearly a million positions with a deeper, slower Classic search, and taught the networks to reproduce those judgements instantly.

This trick is called distillation: an expensive teacher labels the data; a small, fast student learns to approximate the teacher. It works, and it comes with a precise ceiling built in. Over a {{GAMES_PER_MATCH}}-game benchmark, the student and its teacher are statistically level — {{ML_V_CLASSIC_ROUND}}% to {{CLASSIC_V_ML_ROUND}}%. A student that ties its teacher. Which told me something useful: if I wanted a meaningfully stronger opponent, fiddling with network architecture was not the answer. I needed a better teacher.

The twist: it was already solved

In March 2025, Padraig Lamont announced that royalur.net — after seven years of on-and-off effort, and a breakthrough contributed by Jeroen Olieslagers — had strongly solved the Royal Game of Ur.

“Solved” has a precise ladder of meanings in game theory. Ultra-weakly solved: we can prove who wins with perfect play, without knowing how. Weakly solved: we know perfect play from the starting position — that's what happened to checkers in 2007. Strongly solved is the top rung: the best move is known from every legal position, including the messes perfect play would never reach. That is what royalur.net did, for the Finkel rules used here and two other common rule sets.

For the Finkel rules that means roughly 276 million reachable positions (138 million after exploiting symmetry — a community member going by Mr. Carrot pointed out that mirroring the board just swaps the players, halving the storage). You can't crack a dice game the way Connect Four was cracked, by reasoning backwards from final positions: captures send pieces back toward the start, so positions can repeat and the game graph has cycles. The tool that works is value iteration, the workhorse of every reinforcement learning textbook: give every position a guessed win probability, then repeatedly recompute each guess from its successors — averaging over the dice, assuming the mover picks the best continuation — and sweep the whole state space over and over until 276 million numbers stop changing. Those final numbers are not estimates. They are the answer.

Seven years to find the road; in the end, under five hours on a laptop to drive it.

The result is a table holding the exact probability that the player to move goes on to win — for every reachable position, assuming perfect play from both sides ever after. It is 1.6 GB raw, 827 MB compressed, MIT-licensed, and anyone can download it.

The announcement went up on 10 March 2025. My first commit is dated 21 June 2025 — I built Classic and the ML opponent that summer, three months after the answer key was published, and never thought to check whether one existed. Then the project slept for a year. When I came back this July, intending only to give the site a facelift, I finally read around the game properly — and there it was. I'd love to report that my reaction was pure scientific delight. For about ten minutes it was closer to deflation: the cleverest parts of my hobby project, pre-empted before I'd started. Then the obvious reframe arrived — somebody had just handed me the best training data a game-AI hobbyist could ever ask for. Exact. Complete. Free.

The third opponent: distilling perfection

The naive move — ship the table, look every move up — doesn't survive contact with a browser. This site is a small offline-capable web app; asking visitors to download 827 MB of Mesopotamian perfection was not on. But I had just spent a summer on the alternative without realising it: distillation, again. Same trick, infinitely better teacher.

I sampled two million positions from the tablebase, each with its exact win probability, and trained a small value network to reproduce the number. Oracle, the third opponent, is that network: 29,057 parameters — thirty-two inputs describing which squares each side occupies and how many pieces wait off-board or have finished, a few dense layers, and one output. The win probability.

How faithful is the copy? On a hundred thousand positions held back from training, Oracle's average error is 0.34 percentage points of win probability; 95% of positions are within 0.9, and the worst it was caught being wrong was about six. And here's the part I find satisfying: it doesn't need to be told which move to make. The rules engine lists the legal moves; the network values each resulting position; and because the table stores the probability for the player about to move, the arithmetic is one line — a successor is worth 1 − V if the turn passes to the opponent, V if you landed on a rosette and kept it, and 1 if the move wins outright. Highest number plays. No policy network, no hand-tuned bonuses left anywhere.

Did it work?

The main result is not subtle. Oracle beats Classic {{ORACLE_V_CLASSIC_ROUND}}% of the time and ML {{ORACLE_V_ML_ROUND}}%, while Classic against ML remains a coin flip. Two things about this strike me as genuinely instructive.

First, a 29,057-parameter network is thrashing a 164,000-parameter one — not despite being smaller, but because its training labels were better. Same board, same feature-engineering instincts, same WebAssembly runtime; the only meaningful difference is who the teacher was. Data quality beat model size, in miniature.

Second — and this is the number I keep coming back to — Oracle still loses roughly one game in six to an opponent it towers over. That is not a flaw. That is Ur. When every turn starts with four coin flips, perfect play doesn't mean winning; it means never donating a single percentage point of win probability. Luck decides games. Skill decides averages. The ancients built a game where a god could still lose to a lucky child, and the mathematics now confirms it.

What I'm taking away

  1. An AI is defined by its teacher. Classic learned its weights from evolution, ML learned from Classic, Oracle learned from the solved game — and each landed exactly where its teacher could take it. When you want a better model, ask for better labels before you ask for a bigger network.
  2. Distillation is the workhorse of modern AI. Expensive teacher, tiny student, ship the student — it's the same pattern that compresses frontier language models into the ones that run on your phone. Here it's just unusually pure: the teacher is literally perfect, the student is 3,000× smaller, and the price of compression is 0.34 percentage points.
  3. Someone may already have solved your problem — literally. Somebody spent seven years so that I could spend a fortnight. Search for prior work before you start, and again when you pick a project back up after a pause — the state of the art may have moved while you weren't looking. In my case the answer had been published three months before my first commit, and I read it a year later.
  4. “Solved” ruined nothing. The dice see to that: you can play perfectly and still lose one game in six. And the three opponents together turned out to be more interesting than any one of them — a small working museum of game AI, search then imitation then perfection, which you can set against each other in watch mode and see 4,500 years of game meet 75 years of computing.

All three opponents are free to play, right here in your browser, no account needed — and the game works offline. The Oracle will probably beat you. Not always, though. That's the dice — and after four and a half thousand years, they are still the best part.
